questions.question: The three CORE technologies of Web Components are:

options.text: Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, HTML Templates
CSS, JS, HTML (the standard web trio)

questions.explanation: Web Components are built from Custom Elements (new tags), Shadow DOM (encapsulation), and HTML Templates (<template>/<slot>).

questions.question: Custom Elements are defined with:
questions.explanation: customElements.define(name, class) registers a new tag; the class must extend HTMLElement.

questions.question: Which lifecycle callback runs when a custom element is inserted into the DOM?
questions.explanation: connectedCallback fires on insertion; disconnectedCallback on removal; attributeChangedCallback on observed attr change.

questions.question: To react to attribute changes you must:
questions.explanation: observedAttributes getter lists tracked attributes; attributeChangedCallback then fires on their changes.

questions.question: HTML <template> is used because:

options.text: Its content is inert (not rendered) until cloned into the DOM
It renders immediately like a div

questions.explanation: <template> holds markup that isn't displayed; you clone its .content (DocumentFragment) to instantiate UI repeatedly.

questions.question: Web Components differ from Angular/Vue components in that they:

options.text: Are framework-agnostic standard APIs usable anywhere

questions.explanation: Web Components are native browser standards — no framework required and interoperable across frameworks.

questions.question: A challenge with Web Components in SPAs is:

options.text: Server-side rendering / hydration support is less mature than framework components

questions.explanation: SSR/hydration and advanced tooling (like Angular's DI) integrate less seamlessly with raw Web Components.

questions.question: Angular Material icons often render via:
questions.explanation: mat-icon with svgIcon uses SVG, a common Web Component/icon pattern — scalable and styleable.
